title: SG-0 Exam Toolkit
html:
Formula sheet, constants, selection trees, rules, traps, and exam strategy

How to use this file. This is the one file to print or keep open in the final week. It collects what the 18 category guides teach. Formulas marked [Sheet] appear on the IASSC Examination Reference Document (version 1.4.2, March 2020, reviewed for this project). Formulas marked [Know] do not, so you must remember them. Confirm the version used in your exam through the official mock exam.

1. Exam facts to confirm at booking

  • 100 questions, 3 hours, closed book, 70% to pass (PeopleCert and IASSC sources).
  • About 20 questions come from each of the five domains (Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control). IASSC does not publish per-topic weights.
  • Calculators are permitted (a scientific calculator, per the instruction page of a past exam form). The reference document is provided on screen. Outside copies are not allowed. True/False questions use A for True and B for False.
  • Some forms may include ungraded items. You cannot tell which, so treat every question as graded.
  • Questions go up to the Evaluate level, so expect scenarios, not only definitions.

2. What is and is not on the reference sheet

Reviewed: IASSC Examination Reference Document version 1.4.2 (March 2020). Confirm the version used in your exam through the official mock exam.

On the sheet: formulas

  • Descriptive: population and sample mean, weighted mean, grouped-data mean, range, mean deviation, population and sample variance and standard deviation.
  • Hypothesis tests: 2-sample t (Welch with df; pooled), 2-sample Z (equal and unequal known σ), test of a mean with known σ, ANOVA correction factor and sums of squares (SS total as Σ(y − ȳ)², SS treatment three ways), χ² for a variance, F for variances, 1-sample t, paired t, pooled variance, 1-proportion z, 2-proportion z (unpooled).
  • Intervals: two proportions, two means with known σ, paired sample, pooled t (equal variance, n under 30), Welch t.
  • Regression: correlation coefficient, simple and multiple regression equations, multiple standard error.
  • Capability: CI for Cpk, Cpk from attribute data, Cp, Cpk via Z upper and Z lower, standard error of Cpk.
  • Control charts: c, np, p (average n), u (average n), Xbar-R, Xbar-S, CuSum (standardized), EWMA.

On the sheet: tables

  • Z: a left-tail table (Z = −4.9 to 0.0), and a second table titled "Right Tail Area" for Z = 0.00 to 4.9 that actually lists the area to the left of Z (0.50000 at Z = 0.00, 0.97500 at Z = 1.96).
  • t: Table 1 with columns 0.600 to 0.995 (cumulative, equal to 1 − α); Table 2 with columns for one-tail α (0.25 to 0.005) and more decimals. df 1 to 30, 40, 60, 120, infinity.
  • F: upper-tail values for α = 0.05, α = 0.01, and α = 0.10, each in two parts. Columns are numerator df, rows are denominator df.
  • χ²: right-tail columns 0.995 to 0.500 and 0.250 to 0.001; df 1 to 30, then 40 to 100 by 10.
  • Control chart constants for n = 2 to 25: A2, A3, d2, D3, D4, B3, B4. (There is no c4.)

Not on the sheet: know it, or expect it in the question

  • I-MR formulas (they follow from the n = 2 row of the constants table, see section 4).
  • c4, so σ = S̄ ÷ c4 needs the constant supplied.
  • Western Electric and Nelson rules.
  • The sigma, DPMO, and yield conversion table.
  • DPU, DPO, DPMO, FTY, RTY, PCE, Little's Law, takt time.
  • FMEA RPN and the C&E matrix score.
  • Gage R&R, %Study Var, %Tolerance, ndc, kappa.
  • ANOVA df, MS, and F.
  • Regression slope and intercept, R², adjusted R², VIF, interval formulas.
  • Binomial and Poisson formulas.
  • Sample-size formulas.
  • Chi-square contingency expected counts and df.
  • Rank-test procedures (Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis, Mood's, Friedman, sign, Wilcoxon).
  • Box-Cox, kanban count, ROI, and payback.

Sheet quirks to remember

  • The 2-proportion z on the sheet is unpooled. Software usually pools.
  • The p and u chart limits on the sheet use the average subgroup size.
  • The Cpk attribute formula builds in the 1.5 shift: Cpk = (1.5 + Z of proportion good) ÷ 3.
  • Cp and Cpk are written with the sample standard deviation s.
  • The Z table titled "Right Tail Area" lists area to the left. For a right tail, use 1 minus the value, or the left-tail table at −Z.
  • t Table 1 is headed "Alpha Risk" but its columns equal 1 − α. Table 2 columns are true one-tail α.
  • Some df subscripts are generic ("n − 1"). Pooled 2-sample df = n1 + n2 − 2.
  • One pooled-t entry appears to print s_p without a square root and calls it the pooled variance. The t statistic needs the pooled standard deviation, the square root.
  • The CuSum on the sheet is standardized (divided by σ). The EWMA entry prints the λ range backwards; λ should be greater than 0 and at most 1.

3. Master formula sheet

Six Sigma metrics [Know]

  • DPU = defects ÷ units
  • DPO = defects ÷ (units × opportunities per unit)
  • DPMO = DPO × 1,000,000
  • FTY = units passing a step the first time ÷ units entering. Approximately e^(−DPU) only if defects are random (Poisson).
  • RTY = FTY1 × FTY2 × ... × FTYn. RTY is never above the lowest step FTY.
  • Normalized yield = RTY^(1/n) (extension)
  • Takt time = available time ÷ customer demand
  • Process cycle efficiency = value-added time ÷ total lead time
  • Little's Law: lead time = WIP ÷ throughput rate
  • Sigma level (short-term Z) = long-term Z + 1.5. Long-term Z comes from the Z table using DPMO ÷ 1,000,000 as the tail area.

Descriptive statistics [Sheet]

  • Mean: x̄ = Σx ÷ n; population μ = ΣX ÷ N
  • Weighted mean = Σ(w·x) ÷ Σw
  • Grouped mean = Σ(f·X) ÷ n (X = class midpoint)
  • Mean deviation = Σ|X − x̄| ÷ n
  • Sample variance s² = Σ(X − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1); population σ² = Σ(X − μ)² ÷ N
  • s = σ(n) × √[n ÷ (n − 1)]
  • Range = highest − lowest. IQR = Q3 − Q1 [Know]
  • z = (x − μ) ÷ σ [Know]
  • Variances of independent variables add: σ²total = σ²1 + σ²2 [Know]
  • Observed variation: σ²obs = σ²process + σ²measurement [Know]

Probability and distributions [Know]

  • P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)
  • P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A). If independent, P(A) × P(B).
  • P(B | A) = P(A and B) ÷ P(A)
  • At least one = 1 − P(none)
  • Binomial: P(x) = nCx · pˣ · (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ˣ; mean np; SD √[np(1 − p)]
  • Poisson: P(x) = e^(−λ) · λˣ ÷ x!; mean = variance = λ
  • Exponential: P(time beyond t) = e^(−t ÷ mean)

Inference and sample size [Know]

  • Standard error of a mean = s ÷ √n (σ ÷ √n when σ is known)
  • CI for a mean: x̄ ± t(α/2, n − 1) × s ÷ √n
  • CI for a proportion: p̂ ± z × √[p̂(1 − p̂) ÷ n]
  • CLT: sample means have SE = σ ÷ √n
  • Sample size for a mean: n = (Z × σ ÷ E)²
  • Sample size for a proportion: n = Z² × p(1 − p) ÷ E² (use p = 0.5 if unknown)
  • 1-sample t sample size: n ≈ (Zα/2 + Zβ)² × σ² ÷ δ²
  • 2-sample t sample size per group: n ≈ 2 × (Zα/2 + Zβ)² × σ² ÷ δ²

Hypothesis tests

  • 1-sample t [Sheet]: t = (x̄ − μ) ÷ (s ÷ √n), df = n − 1
  • 2-sample t, Welch [Sheet]: t = (x̄1 − x̄2) ÷ √(s1²/n1 + s2²/n2). df = (A + B)² ÷ [A²/(n1 − 1) + B²/(n2 − 1)] with A = s1²/n1, B = s2²/n2
  • 2-sample t, pooled [Sheet]: t = (x̄1 − x̄2) ÷ [s_p × √(1/n1 + 1/n2)]; s_p = √{[(n1 − 1)s1² + (n2 − 1)s2²] ÷ (n1 + n2 − 2)}; df = n1 + n2 − 2
  • 2-sample Z, known σ [Sheet]: z = (x̄1 − x̄2) ÷ √(σ1²/n1 + σ2²/n2)
  • Paired t [Sheet]: t = d̄ ÷ (s_d ÷ √n), df = n − 1
  • χ² for a variance [Sheet]: χ² = (n − 1)s² ÷ σ0², df = n − 1
  • F for two variances [Sheet]: F = s1² ÷ s2², df (n1 − 1, n2 − 1); larger variance on top
  • 1-proportion [Sheet]: z = (p − π) ÷ √[π(1 − π) ÷ n]
  • 2-proportion, sheet form [Sheet]: z = (p1 − p2) ÷ √[p1(1 − p1)/n1 + p2(1 − p2)/n2]
  • CI for difference of proportions [Sheet]: (p1 − p2) ± z × √[p1(1 − p1)/n1 + p2(1 − p2)/n2]
  • Contingency chi-square [Know]: expected = row total × column total ÷ grand total; χ² = Σ(O − E)² ÷ E; df = (r − 1)(c − 1)

ANOVA

  • Correction factor [Sheet]: C = T² ÷ N
  • SS total [Sheet]: ΣX² − (ΣX)² ÷ N, or (N − 1)s²
  • SS treatment [Sheet]: Σ(Tᵢ² ÷ nᵢ) − C, or Σnᵢ·x̄ᵢ² − N·x̿²
  • SS error [Know]: SS total − SS treatment
  • df [Know]: between = k − 1; within = N − k; total = N − 1
  • MS = SS ÷ df; F = MS between ÷ MS within [Know]

Measurement system [Know]

  • GRR = √(repeatability² + reproducibility²)
  • Total variation = √(GRR² + part-to-part²)
  • %Study Var = GRR ÷ total variation × 100
  • %Tolerance = 6 × GRR ÷ (USL − LSL) × 100 (older material used 5.15)
  • %Contribution = GRR variance ÷ total variance × 100
  • ndc = 1.41 × (part SD ÷ GRR SD), truncated; need 5 or more
  • Kappa = (Po − Pe) ÷ (1 − Pe)
  • Guidelines (AIAG as cited by Minitab): GRR under 10% acceptable, 10 to 30% conditional, over 30% unacceptable. Kappa of 0.75 or more is good.

Capability

  • Cp = (USL − LSL) ÷ 6s [Sheet]
  • Zupper = (USL − X̄) ÷ s; Zlower = (X̄ − LSL) ÷ s; Cpk = min(Zupper ÷ 3, Zlower ÷ 3) [Sheet]
  • Cpk from attribute data = (1.5 + Z of proportion good) ÷ 3 [Sheet]
  • CI for Cpk = Cpk ± Zα/2 × √[1 ÷ (9n) + Cpk² ÷ (2n − 2)] [Sheet]
  • Cpu = (USL − μ) ÷ 3σ; Cpl = (μ − LSL) ÷ 3σ [Know]
  • Pp and Ppk use overall σ in place of within σ [Know]
  • Sigma level (short-term Z) = 3 × Cpk [Know]

Regression

  • r = Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) ÷ √[Σ(X − X̄)² × Σ(Y − Ȳ)²] [Sheet]
  • Ŷ = a + bX [Sheet]; multiple: Ŷ = a + b1X1 + ... + bkXk [Sheet]
  • Multiple standard error = √[Σ(Y − Ŷ)² ÷ (n − (k + 1))] [Sheet]
  • Slope b = Sxy ÷ Sxx; intercept a = Ȳ − b·X̄ [Know]
  • R² = SS regression ÷ SS total [Know]; adjusted R² = 1 − (1 − R²)(n − 1) ÷ (n − k − 1) [Know]
  • Regression ANOVA df [Know]: simple = 1, n − 2, n − 1; multiple = k, n − k − 1, n − 1
  • VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − R²j) [Know]
  • Box-Cox λ: 1 = none, 0.5 = square root, 0 = natural log, −1 = reciprocal [Know]

Control charts

  • Xbar-R [Sheet]: X̿ ± A2 × R̄; R chart UCL = D4 × R̄, LCL = D3 × R̄; R̄ = ΣR ÷ k
  • Xbar-S [Sheet]: X̿ ± A3 × S̄; S chart UCL = B4 × S̄, LCL = B3 × S̄
  • np [Sheet]: np̄ ± 3√[np̄(1 − p̄)]
  • p [Sheet]: p̄ ± 3√[p̄(1 − p̄) ÷ n̄]
  • c [Sheet]: c̄ ± 3√c̄
  • u [Sheet]: ū ± 3√(ū ÷ n̄)
  • I-MR [Know, but derivable from the n = 2 constants]: X̄ ± 2.66 × MR̄ (2.66 = 3 ÷ d2); MR UCL = D4 × MR̄ = 3.267 × MR̄; σ = MR̄ ÷ d2 = MR̄ ÷ 1.128
  • EWMA [Sheet]: EWMAₜ = λ·Yₜ + (1 − λ)·EWMAₜ₋₁, with λ greater than 0 and at most 1, and EWMA₀ = target or historical mean
  • CuSum [Sheet]: Sₙ = (1 ÷ σx) × Σ(xᵢ − T), the cumulative sum of deviations from target T, in σ units
  • For attribute charts, a negative lower limit is set to 0.

Lean, risk, and money [Know]

  • Kanban count N = (demand × lead time × (1 + safety factor)) ÷ container size, rounded up
  • RPN = Severity × Occurrence × Detection (each 1 to 10)
  • C&E matrix score = Σ(output importance × relationship rating)
  • ROI = (benefit − cost) ÷ cost
  • Payback = investment ÷ annual benefit

  • Use A2 with R̄ (Xbar-R), A3 with S̄ (Xbar-S), D3 and D4 for the R chart, B3 and B4 for the S chart, and d2 to estimate σ from R̄ (σ = R̄ ÷ d2).
  • c4 is not in the table, so σ = S̄ ÷ c4 needs the constant supplied.
  • I-MR limits from the n = 2 row: X̄ ± 3 × MR̄ ÷ d2 = X̄ ± 2.66 × MR̄; MR chart UCL = D4 × MR̄ = 3.267 × MR̄; LCL = D3 × MR̄ = 0.
  • The point is to find the right column and row quickly, not to memorize digits. Check the table in your version of the document.

6. Hypothesis test selection tree

Decide in this order: data type, number of groups, independent/paired/blocked, parameter (mean or median, variance, proportion), then normality. Check sample size and robustness last.

DataQuestionNormal dataNon-normal data
ContinuousOne sample versus a target1-sample t1-sample sign or Wilcoxon
ContinuousTwo independent groups2-sample tMann-Whitney
ContinuousTwo paired measurementsPaired tWilcoxon on the differences
ContinuousThree or more groupsOne-way ANOVAKruskal-Wallis or Mood's median
ContinuousBlocked or repeated measuresTwo-way ANOVA (recognition)Friedman
ContinuousVariance versus a targetChi-square for a variancenot applicable
ContinuousTwo variancesF testLevene
ContinuousThree or more variancesBartlettLevene
DiscreteOne proportion1-proportionExact binomial if n is small
DiscreteTwo proportions2-proportionFisher's exact if counts are small
DiscreteCategories by categoriesChi-square contingencyChi-square contingency

Reading the decision

  • p below alpha: reject H0. Say "fail to reject," never "accept."
  • Confidence interval for a difference excludes 0: the means differ.
  • Significant ANOVA: at least one mean differs, so follow up with a post-hoc test.
  • Statistically significant is not the same as practically significant.

Phase I: build trial limits (often 20 to 25 subgroups), remove special causes. Phase II: monitor with the established limits.

8. Chart-reading rules

Western Electric

  1. One point beyond 3σ
  2. Two of three beyond 2σ, same side
  3. Four of five beyond 1σ, same side
  4. Eight in a row on one side of the center line

Nelson (Minitab)

  1. One point beyond 3σ
  2. Nine in a row on one side of the center line
  3. Six in a row steadily increasing or decreasing
  4. Fourteen in a row alternating up and down
  5. Two of three beyond 2σ, same side
  6. Four of five beyond 1σ, same side
  7. Fifteen in a row within 1σ of the center line
  8. Eight in a row beyond 1σ on either side

Use one rule set per question. Minitab applies only the beyond-limits test on EWMA and CuSum charts. A 3σ limit gives about a 0.27% false-alarm rate per independent point.

Responding

  • Common cause: leave it alone and improve the system.
  • Special cause: contain, investigate, correct, document.
  • Do not recompute limits because a point is out of control. Recompute only after a verified process change and a stable baseline.
  • Out of control is not the same as out of spec.

9. Top exam traps

  1. Spec limits versus control limits. They are independent.
  2. Defects versus defectives (DPMO, Poisson, c or u charts versus binomial, np or p charts).
  3. "Fail to reject" versus "accept."
  4. Type I (false alarm) versus Type II (missed detection).
  5. Paired versus independent samples.
  6. Final yield versus first-time yield. RTY needs first-time yield.
  7. Prevention (control) poka-yoke versus warning (detection) poka-yoke.
  8. Confidence interval (average) versus prediction interval (one unit).
  9. Stable versus capable. Capability on an unstable process is not valid.
  10. Correlation versus causation. Strong r can come from a lurking variable or one outlier.
  11. Statistical versus practical significance.
  12. Frequency versus cost in a Pareto chart.
  13. Precise versus accurate. Bias, linearity, and stability.
  14. Standard error (σ ÷ √n) versus standard deviation when asked about a sample mean.
  15. Population (σn) versus sample (n − 1) standard deviation on the calculator.
  16. Cp (potential) versus Cpk (centering). Cp much larger than Cpk is a centering problem.
  17. Agreement is not accuracy in attribute MSA.
  18. A fishbone or C&E matrix lists suspects. It does not prove a cause.
  19. Detection is reverse-scaled in FMEA. Severity can outrank RPN.
  20. Round kanban counts up. Set negative attribute-chart lower limits to 0.
  21. Western Electric 8 versus Nelson 9. Do not mix rule sets.
  22. 3.4 DPMO includes the 1.5σ shift. Unshifted ±6σ is about 0.002 PPM.
  23. A significant ANOVA does not name the best group.
  24. A non-significant result with low power means "insufficient evidence," not "no difference."
  25. Tampering (adjusting on common-cause noise) makes variation worse.

10. Exam strategy

Time. 100 questions in 180 minutes is about 1.8 minutes per question. Plan a first pass of about 120 minutes, leaving about 60 minutes to return to flagged questions and review.

Order of attack

  • Answer sure questions fast. Flag anything that needs a long calculation and come back.
  • Read the last sentence first, to know what is being asked, then read the scenario for cue words.
  • Eliminate distractors. On "which test" questions, run the decision order. On "which chart," use the selection tree.
  • For calculations, write the formula, substitute, and check units. Use the reference document for formulas and tables, and memorize what it does not give.

Cue words

  • "Before and after on the same units" points to paired.
  • "Variation decreased" points to a variance test.
  • "Waiting" and "backlog" point to Lean. "Defects" and "inconsistent" point to Six Sigma.
  • "Long-term" or "with the 1.5σ shift" means subtract 1.5 from Z.
  • "Next unit" points to a prediction interval. "Average" points to a confidence interval.

Preparation

  • Get the official mock exam and sample paper from PeopleCert and use them to learn the interface and the question style.
  • In the final week, take timed practice exams under real conditions.
  • Rework every missed question into one line: what the trap was and what the cue word should have told you.

End of SG-0. Remaining pieces: the scenario Q&A and workbook sets, and the build plan for the PWA.
